title.en: Chunking: How RAG Splits Documents (With Overlap)

description.en: Before retrieval comes chunking — the step that quietly makes or breaks every RAG app. Implement the sliding-window chunker LlamaIndex and Haystack use under the hood.

story_variants.en:
## The Step Everyone Skips (and Then Regrets)

"Teams spend weeks tuning their LLM and their vector database," Vaathiyaar sighs, "then discover their RAG answers are bad because of the *boring* step in the middle: **chunking**. Split your documents wrong and the right answer gets sliced in half, landing in no chunk at all."

### Why Chunk At All?

Embedding models have a size limit and retrieval works best on focused passages. So **LlamaIndex**, **Haystack**, and every other 2026 RAG framework break long documents into **chunks** — small windows of text — before embedding them.

### The Overlap Trick

If you cut cleanly every N characters, a sentence spanning a boundary is torn apart and its meaning is lost. The fix is **overlap**: each chunk repeats the last slice of the previous one, so ideas that straddle a boundary survive in at least one whole chunk.

```
text:    "the quick brown fox jumps"
size=10, overlap=3

chunk 0: "the quick "
chunk 1: "k brown fo"   <- 'k ' repeated from chunk 0
chunk 2: "fox jumps"
```

The window slides forward by `size - overlap` each step. Bigger overlap = safer boundaries but more chunks (and more storage and embedding cost). It's the single most important knob in a RAG pipeline, and almost nobody tunes it deliberately.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** when RAG "can't find" an obvious fact, suspect chunking first. The fact was probably split across two chunks and fully present in neither.

Today you implement the exact sliding-window chunker sitting inside those frameworks — `size` characters per chunk, sliding by `size - overlap`.
